artifactEvidence.excerpt: People and organisations using AI professionally have separate duties. Some concern systems that infer emotions from features such as a face or voice, called emotion recognition. Others concern systems that sort people into groups using such features—for example, estimating an age group from a face—called biometric categorisation. These names describe what the systems attempt to do; they do not guarantee that their conclusions are accurate.

Disclosure also covers deepfakes: AI-generated or altered images, audio or video that falsely appear authentic. Some AI-generated public-interest text requires disclosure too; an exception applies when there is human review or editorial control and someone holds editorial responsibility for publication.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: Think of the disclosure as caller ID for particular AI encounters. Seeing who is calling gives you useful information before you pick up. It does not tell you whether the caller’s next sentence will be true.

An AI label has the same limit. It tells you something about how the material was produced; it does not establish whether its claims are correct. Imagine a labelled AI-generated video saying your train line closes tomorrow. The label helps explain where the video came from. The transport operator’s service notice is what you need to check the closure.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: Article 50 of the European Union’s AI Act began applying on August 2, 2026. In covered situations, companies supplying AI systems must tell people when they are interacting with AI. Certain AI-generated or altered outputs must also carry marks that software can detect, even when those marks are not visible to you.

The details depend on who supplies or uses the system and what it does. Certain systems on the market before August 2 have until December 2, 2026 to meet the software-detectable marking requirement. That is a limited transition, not a delay to all the rules.
There are two separate jobs here: signalling AI involvement and checking the underlying claim. The first helps you decide what you are looking at. It cannot do the second for you.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: If you are in the EU, look for disclosure in the situations covered by these rules. A label is useful information, not a stamp saying “verified”. For a claim you might act on, open the original source and check its date and exact scope. In the train example, that means confirming which line, which stations and which day.

An absent label does not prove that something was made by a human or that it complies with the rules. If you supply or use AI professionally, consult the Commission’s guidance for your exact role and use; this short explanation is not a complete compliance checklist.

summary: A well-executed dated news explainer: it states the change and its scope precisely, uses one earned analogy to make the label's epistemic limit memorable, preserves limitations throughout, and lands on concrete, bounded actions; no failure family is present.
strengths: The caller-ID analogy does real explanatory work, teaching the origin-versus-truth distinction and returning cleanly to the AI-label mechanism (P006–P008).
Limitations are consistently preserved: labels do not verify claims, absence of a label proves nothing, and the piece disclaims completeness as compliance guidance (P003, P010).
Next actions are concrete and worked through the train example—confirm which line, which stations, which day (P009).
Scope and timing are precise, distinguishing the August 2 application from the December 2 marking transition without overstating either (P005).
